event: VXE 466 deviated from course after recovery handoff during a flight in falling snow, then flew on until it hit terrain and was lost.
failure_mode: suspected blockage of the pitot tube by snow or freezing rain, giving false airspeed to the autopilot
contributing: flight continued into snow, outside published environmental limits
no heated pitot and no GCS icing-temperature warning
loose static probe found on the ADP during bench test (judged unrelated)

evidence.quote: It had started snowing during the flight which lead them to start a landing.
Investigation complete, Incident Report created ready for Review. Following tests support the snow clogged the pitot tube theory.
Passed wind tunnel test up to 60fps.
Production test checked out fine. Static probe was coming out of ADP when disconnecting cube from static probe.
The “event” is probably a mechanical shift of some sort, like a wing tip that rotates.”

team_root_cause: Operation of aircraft outside published environmental limitations. Probable cause snow or freezing rain block the pitot tube

would_settle_it.what: the log plots of IAS against GPS ground speed, trims and power before and after the UTC 182300 event, to show airspeed reading low while the aircraft was not slowing
the customer-side investigation and the final report attached there
IAS, OAT and pitot pressure channels around UTC 182300 to confirm a blockage signature rather than a mechanical shift

reasoning: Snow started during the flight and the trims then ran away until full power was needed, which fits a false low airspeed from a blocked pitot. The recovered air data pod passed production and wind tunnel tests afterwards, so a hard fault in the pod is unlikely and a temporary blockage that cleared is the best fit. No measurement shows the blockage itself, and one engineer offered a mechanical shift (wing tip rotation) instead, so this stays narrowed to the air data system at low confidence.
notes: The description says the aircraft flew level with power off, while the quoted log reading says full power was needed to hold altitude; these conflict. The ADP was missing for a time and later found on 371CW (VA-477/VA-478 cover the search); VA-486 traveler PDF has no extractable text. VIT2-227 and the incident report pptx are not in the export.

event: VXE 545 lifted about 3 ft at launch, was underpowered and unstable, dipped the right wing and dragged the wing tip before the launch was aborted, with minor wing tip and payload housing damage.
component: lift ESC soft-start circuit MOSFETs Q20-Q23 (Q20 found shorted)
failure_mode: soft-start circuit stayed off (gate at 0 V), starving the motor of current so it made low thrust at low and mid throttle; one soft-start MOSFET (Q20) later failed drain-source short
contributing: launch wizard has no check that flags a lift motor drawing less current than expected
pre-flight launch wizard only exercised motors 1 and 3, and motor 3 drew less power than the others
ESC heat sinking and missing flyback protection noted as weaknesses of the old ESC design

evidence.quote: See plots in the ppt, It is interesting that motor 3 drew less power than the other 3 motors.
@Cameron Chapman While probing the 545 ESC I found that Soft-start circuit MOSFETs were shorted. Upon further investigation, it was found that Q20-one of 4 MOSFETs in parallel was shorted.
I have managed to replicate the issue on end-of-life ESC. The problem occurs when the soft-start circuit does not come ON.
Upon further investigation, we found that Q20 was shorted.
This fault was localized to position 3 ESC.
Root cause narrowed down to the soft-start circuit of the ESC assembly in position 3 (right rear).

team_root_cause: Soft-start circuit in theVXE545 position 3 VTOL ESC was permanently OFF (i.e.. MOSFETs Q20-Q23 Off). This was causing the motor to get less current and deliver lower force. With the Soft start function OFF, the bulk capacitors would be disconnected from the circuit. The motor would operate, but with considerably lower force, as noticed by the customer. [CC1] [CC2] [RB3] [CC4] These components could be have been defective from the manufacturer, or damaged from heat or transients. It is very difficult to determine the cause of damage to integrated circuits. We believe time spent further investig

would_settle_it.what: check R40, R41 and C12 connections and Q20-Q23 for why the soft-start gate stayed at 0 V (open resistor, solder defect, or MOSFET batch issue)

reasoning: Flight data showed motor 3 (right rear) drawing less power in the launch wizard and running near full throttle at launch. On the dyno the returned assembly (S/N C-S100345) made low force until PWM 1500; probing and thermal imaging found soft-start MOSFET Q20 shorted, and shorting the soft-start gate on a stock ESC reproduced the same force curve. Motor THD and phase balance were normal, so the fault sits in the position 3 ESC soft-start circuit; why the gate stayed off was not proven.
notes: An early theory of a potting-contaminated phase solder joint was tested and rejected. The original low-force behavior disappeared after the pair was separated and reassembled, and a later run showed lower torque across the PWM range, which slightly clouds the bench record. VXEP-198 (old date code FDMS86540 MOSFET batch) was linked as background, not shown to apply to this ESC. Customer reported the motor as original to the aircraft (22 flights, 14.1 h).

event: During MoD training on VXE 516 the front right lift motor sounded different and higher pitched in the launch wizard test; engineers found nothing wrong.
contributing: no manual or training guidance on normal versus abnormal lift motor noise

evidence.quote: Noise sounds normal to me. Nothing that would cause me to be concerned.
Also Plotted the boom currents during LW tests, and current spike magnitudes look normal (~4A sustained).
The SCO and flight ops personnel I asked also are not concerned with this noise.
They do not see any cause for concern based on the sound of the motor / rotor in the video.

team_root_cause: No clear way for operator to identify good vs bad motor assemblies.
reasoning: Several engineers and flight ops staff reviewed the video and judged the noise normal, and boom current plots from the launch wizard showed normal spike magnitudes. No hardware fault was reported, so the report reflects a normal motor sound the operator had no reference for, which matches the team's view that operators lack criteria for good versus bad motors.
notes: Current sensors were not zeroed in the data, which the engineer judged unrelated. Video, AAR and current plot were not converted.

event: VXE 426 overshot its landing zone by more than 150 m on VTOL landing approaches, getting worse over time; no crash is recorded on this ticket.
component: ublox GPS receiver update rate to VTOL AP (INS acceleration correction)
failure_mode: GPS update rate to the VTOL autopilot dropped below the expected rate, corrupting the GPS acceleration correction and giving about 10 degrees pitch estimation error, so the aircraft did not pitch up enough to stop on transition
contributing: VTOL AP heading differs from fixed-wing heading by 5 to 20+ degrees after magnetometer calibration
possible magnetic interference at the calibration site
landing pattern too short for the controller to converge before transition

evidence.quote: Pitch estimation error is ~10 degrees during approach transition when pitch up should arrest forward velocity.
Root cause was found to be a reduction in GPS rate on the ublox receiver.
The differences between fixed-wing and vtol heading estimates are typically quite large (5-20+ degrees in the logs I looked at).
We have discovered a software issue where sometimes the GPS update rate to the VTOL autopilot is too low - 5hz vs. 10hz expected.
We also found some information on a ublox forum that indicates there may be an issue with the M8N where it automatically falls back to 5hz.

team_root_cause:
Created powerpoint here.  Overshoot for this flight appears to be caused in part by attitude estimation errors.  Pitch estimation error is ~10 degrees during approach transition when pitch up should arrest forward velocity.
Root cause was found to be a reduction in GPS rate on the ublox receiver.  See investigation here.

would_settle_it.what: GPS position and velocity update rate (PosRate/VelRate) during the approach, and VTOL versus FWAP heading, to confirm the 5 Hz fallback on this aircraft

would_settle_it.file: SharePoint investigation powerpoint (Root Cause field link)
would_settle_it.what: the report updated in 2025 that ties this overshoot to the GPS rate

reasoning: The team measured about 10 degrees of pitch estimation error during the approach transition, which explains the overshoot. Early comments blamed VTOL magnetometer heading error, but the final Root Cause names a GPS rate reduction on the ublox receiver, the same mechanism worked out on VXEP-427 (5 Hz instead of 10 Hz feeding the INS acceleration correction). The GPS rate on this aircraft's own log is not shown in the export, so the result is narrowed to the GPS rate path with medium confidence.
notes: The attached AAR pack is dated 240417, the date of the VXEP-365 fence crash on the same tail (FS2-1753 covers that slow descent), so the ticket may be using that flight's data. Root Cause field links to a powerpoint not in the export.

VTOL logs almost completely missing and no FDR for the incident flight
elevator not found for inspection after return

evidence.quote: It looks like the FW AP took control of the AC, but promptly proceeded to crash. Some things to track down, elevator failure, airspeed calibration issue, fwd ESC/motor assembly.
Given the receipt inspection damage and that all 3 wires are ripped off, it seems likely this damage was from the crash.
re-terminated output side of boost board with new wires and ODU and board is functioning properly
Per @David Grosher suspected mechanical failure but unable to determine due to extensive aircraft damage.
This investigation did not produce a conclusive root cause.

team_root_cause:
Previous evidence points to a faulty boost board however the issue can not be replicated:
Possible root causes

would_settle_it.file: VXEP-414 VXE 468 Crash After Transition to Forward Flight.pptx
would_settle_it.what: the XComm plots of elevator command versus pitch, airspeed and cruise motor current at the transition
any surviving VTOL AP records around the handover to the FW AP

would_settle_it.file: elevator servo, elevator boost board harness and forward ESC/motor
would_settle_it.what: pre-crash damage on the elevator servo and cruise ESC/motor, including the missing elevator

The elevator boost board failed bench tests at first but worked normally once its torn output harness was re-terminated, and the torn ODU wires most likely came from the crash. event: VXE 538 dropped from a paused hover during a training landing at about 20 ft, behaved erratically, hit the ground, slid and bounced before landing about 10 m off the LZ, damaging the aft landing pad.
component: AS150 power contact (center wing HLB connector, dual current sense assembly)
failure_mode: high contact resistance (435 microohm against a 235 microohm limit) with connector distress, causing HLB voltage to sag below 18 V under about 150 to 180 A lift load
contributing: long paused hover (under 100 s) at high lift current
aircraft built with contacts from before the improved supplier (about Oct 2023)
frayed anti-spark ring on the connector
unexplained cancellation of the pause command

evidence.quote: This looks like an electrical issue given the dip in the HLB to 18 volts.
The center wing power connector exhibits signs of distress. The HLB for that flight showed no signs. The resistor on the center wing connector was measured at 5.7 ohms.
I see the power connector with black plastic peeled and frayed. This makes me think that the power connector was the issue.
that part appears to be the cause of this issue and the only electrical damaged part.
The rapid descent definitely looks related to the battery issue.

team_root_cause:
Suspected: This seems to be the difficult and predicted case of contacts that passed initial testing, but then failed later due to increased resistance (possibly due to plating issues or faulty parts).
AS150 Pin test Results (<235uOhm is pass):
- First test: 435uOhm - FAIL
- 2nd Test after cleaning: 317uOhm - Fail
- 3rd Test after cleaning again: 232uOhm - Pass (Barely)

Aircraft was invoiced 8/11/23, and built with parts before that. The improved supplier was established ~Oct 2023. It did pass our resistance check, but that could be evidence that it is batch related (all aircraft before ~Oct/

would_settle_it.what: why the pause was cancelled at about 20 ft, and whether it coincides with the voltage drop

attachments_read: 21508_RMA Repair Quote for AC VXE-538 Warranty LM UK MOD 7-1-2024.pdf.md
reasoning: The HLB voltage dipped to about 18 V about 10 s before the reported behavior, and the field inspection found the center wing power connector distressed while the HLB side was clean. On return the AS150 pin resistance measured 435 microohm (fail), 317 after cleaning and 232 after a second cleaning, and the dual current sense assembly was replaced as the only damaged electrical part. The descent is tied to the power loss; why the pause was cancelled remains open.
notes: Manufacturing quality is the team's suspected batch cause (pre-Oct 2023 contacts), not proven. Induction PDF has no extractable text. Related collector VXEP-553 and CA ticket VXEP-12 not read.

event: VXE 539 failed to launch on three attempts during a training sortie, aborting before or just after lift motor spin-up with a lift power fault message; no damage.
component: XComm to VTOL AP SAFE OFF command (CAN MAVLink message, no delivery confirmation)
failure_mode: SAFE OFF command not received by the VTOL AP before the first launch, so the launch trigger failed on the safe check and the VTOL AP entered an RTL loop that aborted the next launch
contributing: GCS launch wizard reset does not reset the VTOL AP
logging bug (non-static safelast variable) hides whether SAFE OFF was sent
1 to 3 CAN timeouts logged between XComm and VTOL AP

evidence.quote: [13:06:55.736 831.736] mc launch trigger fail: safe
The first launch failed because the CAN message to disable SAFE mode wasn’t received by the VTOL autopilot.
This unfortunately does not reset the VTOL autopilot which was still in an RTL
My conclusion is that this vehicle CAN bus is working properly.
I saw nothing that would point to a hardware issue on the CAN bus. The CAN signals looked healthy and the wiring looked good.
In the function below the variable ‘safelast’ should be declared as a static variable.

team_root_cause: A missing SAFE off command from XComm to VTOL AP prevented first launch and put the VTOL AP into an RTL loop which prevented second launch.

would_settle_it.what: XComm event log entries showing whether SendSafetySwitch(false) ran before the first launch

attachments_read: 25211_RMA MOD KIT Quote for AC Qty 7 Fuse Expanded Payload  LM TIQ UK MOD 12-4-2024 RMA 241204-1 Job S00146-00001 v.2.pdf.md
reasoning: The VTOL AP event log shows the first launch rejected with 'mc launch trigger fail: safe', and the VTOL CSV shows SAFE mode switched off for motor tests but not before arming. The VTOL AP then sat in an RTL loop that a GCS reset did not clear, so the second launch landed itself immediately. A 53-minute CAN capture and EE inspection found the bus healthy, so the failure is the unconfirmed SAFE OFF messaging in software, though why that one message was lost is not proven.
notes: The third launch attempt followed a full power cycle and still showed the RTL message; the report does not fully explain it. FW AP also reported an IMU error check failure and the first sensor calibration failed; neither was pursued. Jason recreated the symptom on HIL by commenting out SendSafetySwitch(false).

event: On two landings (4 and 5 June 2024) VXE 489 swung direction and lost altitude after the transition to VTOL, then recovered and landed normally.
component: VTOL AP motor command logic with lift ESC firmware (motor 3 sent to standby/brake before full throttle)
failure_mode: motor 3 slow to spool up on landing transition (1.2 to 3.1 s delay) because a VTOL AP flag dropped its command to idle before stepping to 93 percent, interacting with ESC startup
contributing: motor 3 assembly tested noisy and distorted (production reject, back EMF distortion)
ESC sensitive to noise and possible microchip Rev L comparator errata
4 June event also influenced by stronger than reported tailwind (10 to 13 mph)

evidence.quote: See chart 7, it appears that motor 3 is not drawing any current during the excursions, almost like it has a startup lag.
Motor test 1. Motor #1 started immediately, #2 immediately, #3 2-second delay, #4 immediately.
Found flag state(s) in the vtol FW on motor 3 which brought down throttle command to idle before sending it to 93% causing the delay in current draw seen specific to motor 3.
I don’t understand the analysis or the corrective action here, more detail will need to be added to the report to connect the dots
Root cause analysis/corrective actions for the slow motor startup are ongoing but this investigation is closed.

team_root_cause: VTOL AP process of commands to motors with existing configuration and settings in ESC FW is causing a delay.  See report for details.

would_settle_it.what: the VTOL FW flag state forcing motor 3 to idle before the 93 percent command, against motor 3 current
slides 20 and 21 dyno replay data reproducing the delay with flight inputs
motor 3 throttle and boom current at the 5 June transition

attachments_read: 44562_Warranty RMA-001011 Lockheed Martin - VXE-489 Propeller Blade, Landing Pad Repair (RMA 240726)_Signed.pdf.md
reasoning: Flight logs showed motor 3 (right rear) drawing no current during the excursions, and LM motor tests saw a 2 s start delay on motor 3, though Edge could not reproduce it on the iron bird. Later analysis found a VTOL firmware flag that dropped motor 3 to idle before commanding 93 percent, and dyno replay of the flight inputs reproduced delays; the motor itself also tested noisy. The lead flight software engineer did not accept the analysis and the closing note says root cause work continues, so this is narrowed to the VTOL AP command path and motor 3 ESC startup at low confidence.
notes: Two events on this ticket: the 4 June event was first attributed to tailwind and an autopilot-commanded altitude loss before transition; the 5 June event is the main one. Comments mix up 'V589' and 'V489' in one update. Motor 1 restarted on first command during iron bird tests. The RMA quote replaces the right rear lift motor and ESC (107-101631). ENG-3040 is a 2023 forward-rotor start delay on the same fuselage with a different wing set.

event: VXE 430 drifted off its landing pattern on two landings (31 May and 11 June 2024), once by about 2 km, with the operator unable to take manual control, before landing with minor damage.
component: ublox M8N GPS receiver update rate to VTOL AP (INS acceleration correction)
failure_mode: GPS update rate fell to 5 Hz against 10 Hz expected, so the GPS acceleration correction to the INS was wrong and the aircraft did not pitch up enough at transition, arriving in VTOL far too fast and overshooting
contributing: software assumes 10 Hz in the acceleration correction
more GNSS signals enabled in software 1.54.02 likely makes the receiver fallback more common
long orbiting descent before the approach
GCS showed a misleading 'Climb abort, lift system fault' message and the operator could not nudge

evidence.quote: this looks like the same GSP update rate issue.
See slide 5 but basically the vehicle has the power setting too low because it’s going way too fast when VTOL is engaged.
We have discovered a software issue where sometimes the GPS update rate to the VTOL autopilot is too low - 5hz vs. 10hz expected.
We also found some information on a ublox forum that indicates there may be an issue with the M8N where it automatically falls back to 5hz.
Software update in work for GPS update rate issue.

team_root_cause: Root cause of overshoot is a lower than expected GPS update rate.  This low update rate causes the GPS acceleration corrections to the INS to be incorrect, which in turn causes the vehicle to not pitch up enough during transition.

would_settle_it.what: GPS update rate and pitch estimate during the 11 June approach to confirm the 5 Hz signature on that flight
the summary slides showing the GPS rate evidence for this aircraft

reasoning: The flight software engineer reviewed this aircraft's logs and found the same low GPS update rate signature seen on other overshoots, with the vehicle far too fast when VTOL engaged, which also explains the climb fault abort called during landing. The team traced it to the GPS rate to the VTOL AP being 5 Hz instead of 10 Hz, which corrupts the INS acceleration correction, and a ublox M8N fallback to 5 Hz is the suspected trigger. The log plots themselves are not in the export, so confidence is medium.
notes: Two incidents on this ticket (31 May with the climb fault abort and RTB, 11 June with a 2 km drift); the root cause is applied to both. Why the receiver drops to 5 Hz is not established. VXEP-315 and VXEP-412 are related overshoot cases; VXEP-315 not read.
